failure_modes: Spike‑in non‑representativity: spike‑in differs in surface epitopes, density, membrane robustness, or capture-reactivity such that its recovery/protection behavior does not track endogenous EVs—leading to false pass (secretome misclassified as EV‑enriched) or false fail (true EV lot missed). (evidence: ev-misev2023-quality-framework)

Epitope masking / sample‑specific suppression: endogenous EV epitopes can be masked by bound proteins, lipids, or formulation components or degraded during pre‑analytic handling, producing negative endogenous capture despite validated spike‑in recovery (false negatives). (evidence: ev-misev2023-quality-framework)

Co‑elution of non‑vesicular particles: protein aggregates, lipoproteins, or other non‑vesicular nanoparticles bearing the same capture epitopes or binding capture reagents can co‑elute with particle peaks and show apparent detergent/protease protection (partial), generating false positives. (evidence: ev-misev2023-quality-framework)

Assay interference from buffers/labels: fractionation, capture/elution buffers or tracer labels may alter capture efficiency or protease/detergent action, causing inconsistent spike‑in recovery or altered protection readouts that prevent controlled discrimination across lots. (evidence: ev-misev2023-quality-framework)

Low material yield / sensitivity floor: bounded fractions may have insufficient particle mass to detect endogenous capture signals reliably; spike‑in may still be detectable (because of higher input or different detectability), producing misleading discordant readouts. (evidence: ev-hermann-2023-neonatal-hi)

Inconsistent spike‑in recovery across replicates: batch variability in spike‑in QC, addition timing, or fractionation efficiency yields inconsistent internal control behavior that invalidates per‑lot pass/fail calls. (evidence: ev-misev2023-quality-framework)

Incomplete discrimination by detergent/protease: some non‑vesicular complexes or strongly bound proteins may resist protease or show partial detergent sensitivity, making the protection readout ambiguous. (evidence: ev-misev2023-quality-framework)

Translatability/operational mismatch: downstream decisions (e.g., in vivo bridging or delivery route expectations) may be confounded because in vitro identity gate does not predict in vivo recoverability or biodistribution (e.g., intranasal retention and negligible brain uptake in NHPs), causing misprioritization of lots that pass the gate but fail biological bridging studies. (evidence: ev-driedonks-2022-macaque-biodistribution)
strongest_objection: The single strongest bounded objection is that the exogenous intact‑EV spike‑in will not faithfully model endogenous EVs in the program material, so the assay will validate spike‑in recovery while failing to detect (or falsely declaring) endogenous EV enrichment. Concretely, an orthogonal spike‑in may differ in marker display, density, detergent/protease sensitivity, or buffer tolerance such that (A) spike‑in is recovered, protected, and lost on detergent but endogenous EVs are epitope‑masked, low‑abundance, or co‑eluting non‑vesicular particles that either evade capture or mimic protection. This yields systematic false positives (calling secretome preparations “EV‑enriched” because the spike‑in behaved) or false negatives (calling true EV lots “secretome‑like” because endogenous markers were suppressed), undermining the gate’s intended discrimination and any downstream CMC decisions.
